Every Knowl process writing more than about 1200 knowledge items segfaulted, and

same probe crashes on 2.6.0.

native state for every statement past the first inside one transaction. Measured,
same rows, same table, same connection:

  1 statement  x 2400 transactions   2400 inserts   clean
  2 statements x 1200 transactions   2400 inserts   SEGFAULT
  2 statements x 1200, BEGIN/COMMIT  2400 inserts   clean

transaction. Knowl writes an item and its assertion together, so every single
knowledge write is a two-statement transaction. 0.45.2 is the latest release;
there is no upgrade to take.

transaction is clean. Only the second statement inside the wrapper crashes.

ordinary connection -- a SQLite transaction belongs to the connection, so the
statements inside it are inside the transaction and the callback bodies are
unchanged. Applied to createKnowledgeItem and updateKnowledgeItem, the two writers
on the per-write path. The other five transaction sites are batch or maintenance

feat(workspace): report conflicts and duplicates across linked repos

Duplicate and conflict detection only ever looked in the writing repo's own
database, so two linked repos could hold contradictory active knowledge with
nothing noticing. This is the capability the shared-database design was going to
provide, and it needs no shared database -- only the ranker and the conflict
lookup pointed at a peer, which the preceding tasks made possible.

Reports, never mutates. The colliding item belongs to another repo and only that
repo can retire it; a write here superseding it is the failure a single owner per
item exists to prevent, and assertOwnedItem already refuses it on the update
path. Bounded and non-fatal: three candidates per peer, unreadable peers skipped,
any failure degrading to no report rather than a failed write. Outside a
workspace it costs one null check. Both writers are wired, and the batch path
resolves the workspace once rather than once per atom.

Found on the way, and fixed here because this feature depends on it: an
exclusive conflict key with no scope has never been detected. eq(column, null)
renders `conflict_scope = NULL`, and nothing equals NULL in SQL, so the simplest
way to declare "only one active answer to this" matched nothing and guarded
nothing. Two sites had it -- checkKnowledgeConflict and the guard inside
createKnowledgeItem -- and fixing only the first would report the conflict while
still allowing the write. Every existing test supplied a scope, which is why it
went unnoticed.

The batch test also needed per-test directories: a surviving API database made
its write a verbatim no-op of the previous test's, and a no-op reports no
overlap because nothing was written. That read as the batch path being unwired.

fix(workspace): close the join safety gap and stop burning unused repo names

`workspace join` -- adopting a manifest copied from another machine -- skipped every
check `workspace add` applies. A second machine could link the same workspace under a
different embedding model, producing two disjoint vector spaces whose repos simply never
saw each other's items, with nothing reporting why. It also skipped the nesting check and
the Git-tracked-config guard. All three now run through a shared `assertSafeToLink`, before
the local manifest is written, so a refusal leaves no trace of a workspace this repo did
not join. `join` gains `--force` to match `add`.

A removed repo name was retired unconditionally. Retirement protects authorship -- the name
is the ownership key on every item its repo wrote -- but that reasoning needs items. A repo
that owned nothing attached its name to no knowledge, so retiring it bought no safety and
burned the obvious name forever. Retirement is now conditional on ownership, and the repo
whose database still owns items under a retired name can reclaim it by re-linking; no other
repo can, since only the original's database carries that evidence.

README: both routes into a workspace now document the same guarantees, and the ownership
limitation section is replaced -- writes have been stamped since 2aa7f92.
